new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is root-initial: it falls on the first syllable of the root, so prefixes (including reduplicative and reciprocal prefixes, as in ang-me-'mengen-ai) are unstressed; the one stated exception is adverbs formed from causative a- + adjective, where the prefix carries the stress ('a-ro 'well').
new_statements.exceptions: Adverbs derived from an adjective plus the causative prefix a-: the prefix receives the stress ('a-ro 'well').
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('the root of a word'); illustrated with a prefixed/reduplicated verb form; brief orientation section of a grammar sketch, data from Umbukul village (New Hanover) 1986-88; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Fast 1990 describes Tungak as spoken in Umbukul village (western New Hanover), the SIL project base; same language as Stamm's 'Lavongai' (south-coast dialect, 1937-41). Glottolog tung1290 / ISO lcm; alternative names Tungag, Tungak, Lavongai, Lavangai, Dang, New Hanover. No dialect-level glottocode distinction needed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the root; prefixes (reciprocal ang-, reduplicant me-) are unstressed. Exception: adverbs derived from an adjective with the causative prefix a- stress the prefix ('a-ro 'well').
new_statements.exceptions: Adverbs derived from adjective + causative prefix: the prefix takes the stress ('a-ro 'well').
new_statements.identity_note: Fast 1990 data were gathered in Umbukul village (west New Hanover) 1986-88 per the paper's title footnote; Beaumont 1976 treats Lavongai (= Tungak/Tungag) as one of the Northern New Ireland subgroup languages and describes no particular dialect.
